turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Hale, in you come. I took your blood pressure in the corridor because you looked flushed, and it was up, so Dr Okonkwo should see the figures as well as your form.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Flushed, yes, well the corridor's boiling and I'd legged it from the car park, Pauline had the meter running, and the card machine rejected me twice, so I was all wound up, which is a silly way to arrive when all I actually need is this occupational health form for work.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mr Hale, I'm Dr Okonkwo. Sit yourself down. What's brought you in today, in your own words?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): So I work in the council housing office, a desk job, and I mentioned to my manager that my right knee aches, which I now think was a mistake, because they've stopped me doing the stair inspections until a doctor signs this form to say I'm alright for the desk work, even though I sit down nearly all day.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Pauline, I drive him Tuesdays and Fridays. The form's in the blue folder, and he will talk the hind leg off a donkey if you let him.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's quite alright, Pauline, the detail helps. Nurse, what did you get for the blood pressure?
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): First reading, once he was sat, was one hundred and seventy-two over ninety-eight.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): I left it a couple of minutes and did it again. The second was one hundred and sixty-four over ninety-two, and his pulse was seventy-six and regular.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): That is the white coat business, I'm sure of it. It does this every single time I come in, and then I go home and I'm fine, and I feel completely well. If you feel well you assume the machine in the clinic is just being dramatic.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): White coat is ever so common, so I won't jump. How has the knee been for you?

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It's an ache, right knee, across the front, not a stabbing pain. Stairs in the multi-storey make it worse, sitting eases it, and I wouldn't say it's severe, more a nuisance that clicks into my head when I'm walking back from the photocopier.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And how long has the ache been there?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't put a date on it, I'm afraid. Sometime after the clocks went back, or it might have been before, last autumn or the winter, and I genuinely could not tell you which.
[SEG0014] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He was limping a bit at Christmas, when I took him for the turkey. I only see him two days a week, so I miss bits.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Christmas rings a bell, though I was also hauling boxes of files that week, so the limp might have been that. Either way I still can't tell you when it actually started.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the knee lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't lock, and it has never given way. I'm steady on my feet. Pauline's very strict about that.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He is steady. I wouldn't have him driving if he wasn't.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. With those blood pressure numbers, any headache, chest pain, or breathlessness?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache, no chest pain, and I'm not breathless. I feel well in myself, which is exactly why I think this is white coat and not some silent disaster, though I do know people say high blood pressure doesn't announce itself.

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): My dad had a stroke, incidentally, years back, in his seventies. I only say it because it popped into my head, not because I'm building a case. He lived on a good while after.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's useful to know, even in passing. What do you make of these clinic readings yourself?

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I make them out to be nerves. They did a cholesterol at a health check once, and the nurse then said it was borderline, but she never gave me a figure I can remember, and nobody started me on a tablet.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you remember when that cholesterol check was?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. A good few years ago, could be five, could be more, and I haven't a clue about the month.
[SEG0026] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He still buys the full-fat cheese, whatever he says about easing off. Sorry, Graham.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I did try to ease off, Pauline, for about a fortnight, and then Christmas happened. Anyway, that's not why we're here.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Given the clinic readings, and your dad's stroke sitting in the background, I think I'd like to start a small dose of amlodipine today, five milligrams.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. A tablet, today. I wasn't expecting that, if I'm honest, because I feel fine and the form is the thing I came for, and a new tablet might make me woozy at the office, which would be a whole other form.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Before you write it, doctor, he's got a monitor at home. He doesn't use it like he should, mind.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go on, what sort of figures does he get at home?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I used it on Sunday. I thought it said one hundred and thirty over eighty, but no, hang on, I've got the scrap in my wallet, it was one hundred and twenty-two over seventy-eight.
[SEG0033] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he was gabbling and sweaty in your waiting room, same as always. The second clinic one had already come down a bit, hadn't it, nurse?
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): It had. One hundred and sixty-four over ninety-two from one hundred and seventy-two over ninety-eight. Still high, but it was falling while he sat.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I also had a large coffee in the car, which I shouldn't have, and I'd rushed, as I said, so I don't think today is a fair day to judge my blood pressure for the rest of my life and stick me on a tablet forever.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's new information, and it does change things. I suspect white coat hypertension, though I can't be sure from today, so you've talked me out of starting amlodipine.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't start any blood pressure tablets today. I'd rather you check it at home, morning and evening, seated, for a week, and bring the readings in.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I can do that. The monitor's the Omron one from Boots, Pauline set the date on it because I got the year wrong, which is typical, and I'll write them in the notebook if I remember. I might forget the evening one if Match of the Day is on.
[SEG0039] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll remind him on Tuesdays and Fridays. The other evenings he's on his own, so I can't promise those.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's plenty. Use the same arm, sitting quietly for a few minutes first, and don't bother if you've just dashed up the stairs.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Right arm, I assume, that's the one they always use. And what about the knee form, because my manager will be on at me, and Friday is when they wanted it, though Monday would do if the post is slow, which it is round our way.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the knee before I sign anything. Hop on the couch, or just swing round in the chair, whichever is easier.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Chair is easier. The couch is a bit high and I'd make a meal of getting down, and then we'd be here all afternoon, and Pauline's got another client at half twelve.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): No swelling that I can see, and it's not hot. You bend it fully, and it's a bit tender over the front if I press. Nothing worrying there.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Tender, yes, that's the spot, just under the kneecap. It's only the right, the left has always been fine, touch wood, even after that fun run I did and regretted.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): So this is a straightforward ache at the front of the right knee. I don't think you need a scan for it.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, because I hate those machines. My brother had an MRI for his back and he said it was like being posted through a letterbox, and I've got broad shoulders.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll sign the occupational health form to say you're fit for your desk job. I'd lay off lots of stairs for a couple of weeks while it settles.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol helps the knee a bit. I take two of the five-hundred milligram ones, so a gram, not every day, just when I've been on the stairs.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's a sensible dose. Carry on with that as you need it. No anti-inflammatory if you can help it, with the blood pressure question still open.
[SEG0051] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He had ibuprofen in the cupboard from his brother. I told him not to take his brother's tablets.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't take them. I just looked at the box. His name's on it, Derek, which is not me.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Stick to your own paracetamol. Now, for the pressure, a week of home readings, then I want to see you back here with the notebook.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): In a week exactly, or roughly a week? Only I've got a half day Thursday week, and parking is easier then, and if the readings are all normal I don't want to be started on a tablet at that visit either.

[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Book about a week from today, Thursday is fine if that's when you can park. If the home readings are truly normal we still won't start tablets. We'll decide when we see them.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): I can book that at the desk on your way out, Mr Hale. And I'll print a little home blood pressure sheet if you want lines to write on.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes please, lines are better, my handwriting goes walkabout. And can you put morning and evening on it so Pauline can tell me off properly.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nurse Bennett will sort the sheet and the appointment. Anything else worrying you, even if it feels minor?

[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Not medically. The meter in the car park ate my change once last month, but that's the council, and I work for them, so I shouldn't complain, except I will, at the water cooler, at length.
[SEG0060] person_4 (CAREGIVER): We'll be off, then. I'll make sure the notebook actually comes back with him.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lovely. No new tablets today, home readings for a week, and the form will be signed before you leave. Take care, both of you.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

bad.reason: Borderline cholesterol test is supported, but it was done at a health check, not requested by patient.
bad.text: Cholesterol blood test, reported as borderline (type=laboratory, status=completed, requested_by=patient)

omissions.text: Doctor initially proposed starting amlodipine 5 mg today for the raised clinic blood pressure before changing plan after hearing the home reading and circumstances.
Patient reported feeling completely well/in himself despite the high clinic blood pressure.
Patient said he was steady on his feet.
Patient said the right knee pain was not a stabbing pain.
Tender spot was clarified by the patient as just under the kneecap.
Doctor stated he did not think a scan was needed for the knee.
Patient said paracetamol helps the knee a bit.
Patient denied taking ibuprofen that was in the cupboard; caregiver had raised that there was ibuprofen available from his brother.
Follow-up timing was specified as about a week from today, with Thursday acceptable, and the doctor stated that if the home readings are truly normal they still will not start tablets.
